## Loading Libraries

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library("patchwork")
library("broom")
```

## Loading the data

```{r}
brca_raw <- read_csv("data/Breast Cancer METABRIC.csv",
                     na = c("", "NA", "N/A", "?", "null"))
```

## Cleaning Data

This step takes the raw METABRIC data and makes it ready for analysis. First, `clean_names()` and `rename()` give the columns short, consistent names without spaces, such as `age_at_diagnosis` and `os_months`. Next, the `Positve` typo in the ER (IHC) column is corrected to `Positive`, and the `sex` and `cancer_type` columns are dropped because they hold almost the same value for every patient and add no information. Then the categorical variables (such as ER status, HER2 status, chemotherapy and tumour subtype) are converted to factors so R treats them as groups rather than text. Cohort, histologic grade and tumour stage, which were stored as numeric codes, are converted too, with grade and stage as ordered factors and cellularity ordered Low \< Moderate \< High. Finally, a new `age_group` column bins patients’ ages into 10-year intervals with `cut()`. Missing values are left as `NA`, and no rows are removed.

```{r}
# 2. Clean
brca <- brca_raw |>
  clean_names() |>                       # "Age at Diagnosis" -> age_at_diagnosis
  rename(er_status_ihc  = er_status_measured_by_ihc,
         her2_status_snp6 = her2_status_measured_by_snp6,
         pam50_subtype  = pam50_claudin_low_subtype,
         lymph_nodes_pos = lymph_nodes_examined_positive,
         os_months      = overall_survival_months,
         os_status      = overall_survival_status,
         rfs_months     = relapse_free_status_months,
         rfs_status     = relapse_free_status,
         vital_status   = patients_vital_status) |>
  # fix typo in ER (IHC)
  mutate(er_status_ihc = str_replace(er_status_ihc, "Positve", "Positive")) |>
  # drop constant / near-constant columns
  select(-sex, -cancer_type) |>
  # categorical variables -> factors
  mutate(across(c(type_of_breast_surgery, cellularity, chemotherapy,
                  pam50_subtype, er_status_ihc, er_status, her2_status_snp6,
                  her2_status, hormone_therapy, inferred_menopausal_state,
                  integrative_cluster, primary_tumor_laterality,
                  pr_status, radio_therapy, os_status, rfs_status,
                  vital_status, x3_gene_classifier_subtype,
                  tumor_other_histologic_subtype, oncotree_code,
                  cancer_type_detailed),
                factor),
         cohort = factor(cohort),
         neoplasm_histologic_grade = factor(neoplasm_histologic_grade, ordered = TRUE),
         tumor_stage = factor(tumor_stage, ordered = TRUE),
         cellularity = factor(cellularity, levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"),
                              ordered = TRUE)) |>
  # age groups
  mutate(age_group = cut(age_at_diagnosis, breaks = seq(20, 100, by = 10)))
```

The next step is checking if the data has any missing values

```{r}
brca |> summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  arrange(desc(n_missing))
```

## Writing a new clean csv

```{r}
write_csv(brca, "data/brca_clean.csv")
```

```{r}
view(brca)
```

### Pratyush

```{r}
# receptor_profile: HR+/HER2-, HER2+, Triple-Negative
brca <- brca |>
  mutate(
    receptor_profile = case_when(
      her2_status == "Positive" ~ "HER2+",
      er_status == "Negative" & pr_status == "Negative" &
        her2_status == "Negative" ~ "Triple-Negative",
      (er_status == "Positive" | pr_status == "Positive") &
        her2_status == "Negative" ~ "HR+/HER2-",
      .default = NA_character_
    ),
    receptor_profile = factor(
      receptor_profile,
      levels = c("HR+/HER2-", "HER2+", "Triple-Negative")
    )
  ) 
```

### Sanjay

Creating a new variable how many therapies each patient has received. There are 3 therapies in the data set, hormone therapy, chemotherapy and radio therapy. Each of them are labelled as "Yes" or "No". Yes gives a true value (1) and No gives a false value (0). Adding these 3 will give the number of therapies from 0 to 3. That number is converted using a factor() into an ordered category labelled "None","Single","Double", "Triple". Patients with missing data will be given "NA" instead of "None" to ensure missing data is not confused with no treatment.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

brca <- brca |>
  mutate(
    treatment_n = (chemotherapy == "Yes") +
                  (hormone_therapy == "Yes") +
                  (radio_therapy == "Yes"),
    treatment_burden = factor(treatment_n,
                              levels = 0:3,
                              labels = c("None", "Single", "Dual", "Triple"),
                              ordered = TRUE)
  )

brca |> 
  count(treatment_burden)
```

### Jithin

The "mutation_count" column reflects the number of somatic mutations in each tumor, thereby signifying the genomic instability. We have categorized these raw values into ordered categories where "Low" signifies 1-3 mutations, "Moderate": 4-7 mutations, and "High": 8+ mutations. This new "mutation_burden_group" column was engineered to give an interpretable measurement of the mutational intensity and to use the categories as a convenient grouping factor in plots or summaries. The "mutation_count" column is retained to allow quantitative comparisons among different patients.

```{r}
brca <- brca |>
  mutate(
    mutation_burden_group = case_when( mutation_count >= 8 ~ "High",
                                       mutation_count >= 4 ~ "Moderate",
                                       mutation_count >= 1 ~ "Low",
                                       .default = NA_character_
                                       ),
    mutation_burden_group = cut(mutation_count,
                                breaks = c(0, 3, 7, Inf),
                                labels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High")
                                )
    )

view(brca)
```

Grouping and summarizing the data based on the mutated terms allows us to confirm whether the mutation has been executed properly based on the output.

```{r}
brca |>
  group_by(mutation_burden_group) |>
  summarise(
    n   = n(),
    min = min(mutation_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(mutation_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

### Maria

To get the survival variables ready for modeling, we created two new columns from the cleaned clinical data: `os_years` and `event_os`. Since overall survival was originally recorded in months, we divided `os_months` by 12 so the timeline is easier to interpret in years. We also converted the text labels in `os_status` into a simple binary outcome (`event_os`), coding deceased patients as `1` (`n = 1,144`) and living patients as `0` (`n = 837`), while keeping the `528` missing entries as `NA` so they are automatically excluded from our models.

```{r}
# Convert survival time to years and create binary mortality outcome
brca <- brca |>
  mutate(
    os_years = os_months / 12,
    event_os = case_when(
      str_detect(os_status, regex("deceased|1", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ 1,
      str_detect(os_status, regex("living|0", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_
    )
  )
```

### Maria

To see how age, mutation burden, and treatment intensity affect survival across different breast cancer subtypes, we fit separate logistic regression models (`glm()`) for each PAM50 subtype using `purrr` and plotted the resulting Odds Ratios and 95% confidence intervals.

We adapted the functional programming workflow from Lab 6 (`nest()`, `map()`, and `unnest()`) for this. Instead of splitting the data across thousands of genes, we nested the dataset into six groups by `pam50_subtype` and fit a separate model to each using `purrr`. In Lab 6, the outcome was continuous, so linear regression (`lm()`) was used. Here, our survival outcome (`event_os`) is binary (`1 = Deceased`, `0 = Living`), so we used logistic regression (`glm(..., family = binomial)`). We also set `exponentiate = TRUE` inside `broom::tidy()` to convert raw log-odds into Odds Ratios, which are much easier to interpret. Finally, while a volcano plot works well in Lab 6 for screening thousands of genes at once, a forest plot (`geom_linerange()` + `geom_point()`) is a better choice here. With only 18 subtype-level estimates, a forest plot lets us directly compare exact effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals side-by-side against the dashed neutral line (`OR = 1`).

Any point to the right of the dashed line shows higher odds of mortality, while points to the left indicate lower odds, with horizontal bars showing statistical certainty.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Fit logistic regression models predicting mortality across PAM50 subtypes
subtype_models <- brca |>
  filter(!is.na(pam50_subtype),
         pam50_subtype != "NC") |>
  drop_na(event_os,
          treatment_n,
          mutation_count,
          age_at_diagnosis) |>
  group_by(pam50_subtype) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model = map(data,
                ~ glm(event_os ~ age_at_diagnosis + mutation_count + treatment_n,
                      data = .x,
                      family = binomial)),
    tidied = map(model,
                 ~ tidy(.x,
                        conf.int = TRUE,
                        exponentiate = TRUE))
  ) |>
  unnest(tidied) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(
    term_clean = factor(
      case_when(
        term == "age_at_diagnosis" ~ "Age at Diagnosis\n(per year)",
        term == "mutation_count" ~ "Mutation Count\n(per mutation)",
        term == "treatment_n" ~ "Treatment Burden\n(per therapy)",
        TRUE ~ term
      ),
      levels = c(
        "Treatment Burden\n(per therapy)",
        "Mutation Count\n(per mutation)",
        "Age at Diagnosis\n(per year)"
      )
    )
  )

# Forest plot of odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals across PAM50 subtypes
subtype_models |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate,
             y = term_clean,
             color = pam50_subtype)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1,
             linetype = "dashed",
             color = "grey45") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = conf.low,
                     xmax = conf.high),
                 position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
                 linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
             size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 1.8)) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Subtype:",
                        end = 0.9) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2,
                              byrow = TRUE)) +
  labs(
    title = "Mortality Predictors Across PAM50 Subtypes",
    subtitle = "Odds ratios (95% CI) from logistic regression; dashed line: OR = 1",
    x = "Odds Ratio (log10 scale)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: METABRIC Cohort | Outcome: Overall Mortality (1 = Deceased)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

Results:

Across every subtype, older age at diagnosis consistently increases mortality risk (`OR = 1.03–1.09` per year), whereas mutation count has little effect except in Normal-like tumors (`OR = 1.12`, 95% CI: `1.01–1.27`). Most notably, higher cumulative treatment burden seems to significantly mortality odds in LumA patients (`OR = 0.72`, 95% CI: `0.57–0.89`), suggesting that LumA tumors respond especially well to combined therapies compared to more aggressive subtypes like Her2 or claudin-low, where the confidence intervals cross 1.
